**What you should be able to do after this meeting.** Say whether your
project needs IRB review, a data-use agreement, both or neither, and defend
the answer with the branch of Cornell's decision tree it sits on. Name the
date each gate has to start, counted backwards from January. Say what a
fabricated citation is, and what it costs.

::: {.callout-note title="What to take away" appearance="simple"}
Two gates stand between your design and your data. The **IRB** is an ethics
review, and it applies when you interact with people or hold identifiable
information about them and your results leave the course. A **data-use
agreement** is a contract, and the university signs it, not you. Both run on
clocks you do not control.

You do not decide that you are exempt. The IRB issues that determination, and
it issues nothing until every person on the protocol has finished CITI
training. So everyone in this course completes the training, whether or not
their project needs it.

Removing the names is not de-identification. Nothing at moderate risk or
above goes into a public AI tool.

A fabricated citation is a fabrication. Misconduct is caught by outsiders,
from the data file, years later, and the price is the job.
:::

## Due today

Your project's ethics-and-access checklist, signed by every member, before
you leave. And, individually, your CITI human-participants training
certificate on Canvas before meeting 6, Wednesday September 30.

::::

:::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

## What this hour is for

- Two gates stand between your design and your data.
- The IRB is an ethics review and a data-use agreement is a contract.
- Both run on clocks you do not control.
- You leave with the date each one has to start.
- The integrity rules come last because the tools of next week run under them.

::: {.notes}
Ninety seconds. Say that most teams will find they trip nothing, and that
the check is what tells you which teams those are. A team that finds out in
February that it needs a data-use agreement has lost the semester it was
going to run the study in.

Say the shape of the hour once: why the rules exist, the IRB, contracts,
holding the file, integrity, and the calendar. The calendar is the point.
:::

# 1. Why the rules exist

## Every rule was written after a failure

- The Nuremberg Code of 1947 followed the doctors' trial.
- The Tuskegee study ran for forty years and was stopped by a reporter in 1972.
- The Belmont Report of 1979 followed it and named three principles.
- Respect for persons, beneficence and justice are still the frame every board applies.
- The IRB is the machinery that applies them before the study runs.

[The Nuremberg Code, BMJ 313:1448 (1996) · The Belmont Report, HHS (1979) · CDC, the Tuskegee study](https://www.hhs.gov/ohrp/regulations-and-policy/belmont-report/index.html){style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}

::: {.notes}
Two and a half minutes, and without the sermon. Every rule in research ethics
was written after a specific failure, and that is the whole of the history
you need.

Tuskegee is one sentence. Six hundred Black men in Alabama, four hundred of
them with syphilis, followed from 1932 and never treated, including after
penicillin became the standard treatment. It was stopped in 1972 because a
whistleblower went to the Associated Press. A scientist did not stop it.

Belmont's three principles are the frame. Respect for persons is consent.
Beneficence is risks against benefits. Justice is who bears the risk and who
gets the benefit. Every question an IRB asks is one of those three.
:::

## The modern failures involved no needle

- In 2014 Facebook changed the feeds of 689,003 users to test whether moods spread, and published the result.
- The consent form was the terms of service.
- In 2018 a personality quiz taken by 270,000 people reached up to 87 million profiles through their friends.
- The quiz-takers had agreed to something and their friends had agreed to nothing.
- Neither case involved a needle, a lab, or a person who knew they were in a study.

[Kramer, Guillory and Hancock (2014), PNAS 111(24) · Facebook, April 4, 2018](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1320040111){style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}

::: {.notes}
Two and a half minutes. These are the failures that concern this room,
because this room works with data about people it will never meet.

The Facebook study reduced the positive or negative posts people saw for a
week and measured what they posted. The effect was tiny and real. The
consent was a clause in the data-use policy. PNAS published it and then
published an expression of concern.

Cambridge Analytica: a quiz app called This Is Your Digital Life. The people
who took it consented to sharing their own data. The app also took their
friends' data, which the platform allowed at the time. Facebook's own
estimate was up to 87 million profiles.

Do not resolve what made these research here. That is the next slide, and
it is the room's question.
:::

## What made the Facebook study research

- Facebook runs experiments on its feed every day and nobody calls them research.
- Sixty seconds at your table: what was different about this one?
- Then I take three answers.

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Sixty seconds of table talk, then two or three answers from
the room, then the answer told.

The answer. It was designed to produce generalisable knowledge and it was
published, which is the federal definition of research. So the ethics rules
applied to it and they do not apply to an ordinary A/B test. The terms of
service are not informed consent, which is why PNAS issued an expression of
concern.

The Cornell angle, said plainly. One of the three authors was at Cornell.
Cornell's IRB ruled that he was not engaged in human research, because he
only ever saw results and never the individual data. That is the
existing-data branch of the tree you will see in ten minutes, working.

The point to land: the definition turns on the intent to generalise, not on
whether anybody was hurt. Your capstone is written to say something general,
or it is written for one firm. That choice decides which rules apply.
:::

# 2. The IRB

## Two questions decide whether the IRB applies

- Is it research: a systematic investigation designed to produce generalisable knowledge?
- Are there human participants: you interact with people, or you hold identifiable private information about them?
- Teams miss the second half.
- Scraped posts count when individuals are identifiable.
- Purchased consumer records count.

[45 CFR 46.102, the definitions in the Common Rule](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-45/subtitle-A/subchapter-A/part-46){style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}

::: {.notes}
Two and a half minutes. Both questions have to be yes for the IRB to apply.

The first question is the one the Facebook discussion just answered. The
second is the one teams get wrong, because they hear "human participants"
and think of a survey. Identifiable private information about a living
person is a human participant even if you never meet anybody.

Say the two examples slowly. A file of scraped reviews with usernames. A
purchased file of consumer records with addresses. Both are human
participants. Both are the kind of file somebody in this room is about to
download.
:::

## Cornell's tree has a class-project branch

::: {style="font-size:0.84em"}
- Cornell's IRB office publishes the decision tree its own staff use.
- A project whose sole intent is to meet a course requirement is not human participant research.
- A project whose results leave the course is: a publication, a presentation, a thesis, a sponsor's decision.
- A capstone is the second kind.
- A study whose outcomes stay specific to one organisation is not research either, which is last week's private value.
- When in doubt you ask irbhp@cornell.edu, because you do not make the call.
:::

[Cornell IRB, Does your project require an application to the Cornell IRB office? Decision tree 1](https://researchservices.cornell.edu/sites/default/files/2019-05/IRB%20Decision%20Tree.pdf){style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Read the branch in the tree's own words: "Is the sole intent
of the project to meet course requirements, with no intention to use the
results for something other than the course assignment?" If yes, not human
participant research. If no, the project may lead to use of the results
outside the course, and it continues down the tree.

A capstone whose plan is executed in AEM 6992 and presented to a room, or
handed to a sponsor, is outside the course. So the class-project branch does
not rescue you. Say that before anybody hopes it does.

The private-value line is the one to land. The tree has a separate branch
for quality improvement: a study whose outcomes stay specific to one
organisation, whose programmes or services it is meant to improve, is not
research, even though other organisations might use the results. That is
the project written for one firm's decision from last week. The moment the
same project is written to say something about people in general, it is
research. Teams can choose which of these they are. The choice has to be
made before the data is collected, not after.

The last bullet is the rule: the IRB office makes the determination, and
its address is on the slide.
:::

## Existing data has its own tree

- Are the rows about people who may still be living?
- Is the file publicly available?
- Can you link a row to a living person, directly or through a code?
- If you cannot, and the provider is not your collaborator, it is not human participant research.
- What the vendor calls the file is not one of the questions.

[Cornell IRB, Decision tree 2, research involving secondary or existing data](https://researchservices.cornell.edu/sites/default/files/2019-05/IRB%20Decision%20Tree.pdf){style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. This is the tree most of this room is actually on, because most
of you will use existing data.

Walk it. Living people, or it is out. Publicly available, and it is out. Not
public: can you, the recipient, link a row to a person, directly or through
a code the provider holds? If not, and the provider is just providing, it is
not human participant research. If the provider can link and is your
collaborator, it is.

The last bullet is the one to say twice. The tree asks what you can do with
the rows. It does not ask what the vendor wrote on the invoice.
:::

## Which of these needs an application

- An online experiment on a nutrition label with three hundred paid participants, results to your proposal.
- Foot-traffic data from Dewey, aggregated and de-identified before you see it.
- Glassdoor reviews scraped with usernames, to say something about employers in general.
- Firm financials from Compustat.
- Sixty seconds on your strip: which ones go to the IRB office?

::: {.notes}
Two and a half minutes. Start the count-down at sixty seconds. Then tell it.

The first and the third. The experiment interacts with people and its
results leave the course. The scrape is passive observation of public
behaviour online, which the tree lists by name, and the rows are
identifiable. It goes to the office, it will probably come back exempt, and
the office says so, not you. The scrape also trips a second gate, terms of
service, which is twenty minutes from now.

Dewey arrives aggregated and de-identified, which is the existing-data tree
saying no. Compustat is not about individuals at all.

If a strip says all four, that is the common mistake in the other direction,
and it costs a month of waiting for a determination on a file that never
needed one.
:::

## Three levels of review measured in weeks

::: {style="font-size:0.84em"}
- An exemption takes three to four weeks from start to finish at Cornell.
- Expedited review takes four to six.
- The full board takes four to eight and meets on the first Friday of the month.
- You do not decide that you are exempt: the IRB issues that determination.
- A student protocol needs a faculty advisor who answers for it, and that is me, so your draft goes past me first.
- Boards differ on what they call exempt, on turnaround and on whether coursework counts, and a partner at another university means a second review.
:::

[Cornell IRB, the life cycle of an IRB protocol · IRB FAQs · PI eligibility](https://researchservices.cornell.edu/resources/life-cycle-irb-protocol){style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. The weeks are Cornell's own, from the IRB office's page on the
life cycle of a protocol, and they assume a complete submission. An
incomplete one goes back and the clock restarts.

The full board's clock is a calendar, not a queue. It meets on the first
Friday of the month. Miss the deadline for one meeting and the next one is
a month away.

The exempt rule is the one that catches somebody every year. Exempt is a
category the IRB office puts you in. "We decided it was exempt" is not a
category. Submissions go through RASS-IRB.

A student cannot usually be the principal investigator. A protocol needs a
faculty advisor who takes responsibility for compliance, and for this
course that is me. So the draft goes past me before it goes to the IRB, and
the instrument and the consent language come to office hours first.

The last bullet is the awareness line. Different universities' boards draw
the exempt line differently, run at different speeds, and treat coursework
differently. If your project has a partner at another institution, that
institution's board has a view too, and the two boards sort out who reviews
through a reliance agreement, which takes its own weeks.
:::

## Training comes first and it is required

- Every person named on a protocol completes CITI human-participants training, exempt protocols included.
- The IRB issues nothing until the last name on the protocol has finished.
- The course takes two to four hours and lasts five years.
- Everyone in this room completes it and uploads the certificate to Canvas before meeting 6, Wednesday September 30.
- Do it before you know whether you need it, because one teammate who skipped it holds up the whole team.

[Cornell IRB training · IRB news, October 2022: training required for exempt research](https://researchservices.cornell.edu/resources/irb-training){style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}

::: {.notes}
Two minutes, and this slide is protected in the cut order because the
requirement is graded and has to be said in the room.

Say the mechanism once, in the syllabus's words. Register at citiprogram.org
under the Cornell affiliation. Take the course Cornell accepts, which is
called IRB Training or IRB Basic. Download the completion certificate and
upload it to the Canvas assignment by Wednesday September 30 at 11:59 pm.
Not there by then costs five participation points, the same as the research
interest survey.

Say why it is everyone and not just the survey teams. A team that pivots to
a survey in November, which happens, cannot wait for four people to do four
hours of modules while the protocol sits. And the training is the cheapest
thing on this calendar.
:::

# 3. Contracts

## A data-use agreement is a contract

::: {style="font-size:0.84em"}
- It is not an ethics review and it does not replace one.
- The university signs it, through the Office of Sponsored Programs, not you.
- Expect legal review on both sides and expect months.
- It binds Cornell, and it binds you through Cornell, so a breach is the university's problem and then yours.
- OSP is asked at osp_dua@cornell.edu, and whether it will sign for a class project is a question to ask in October, not assume.
:::

[Cornell Research Services, exchange commercially unavailable or restricted data](https://researchservices.cornell.edu/resources/exchange-commercially-unavailablerestricted-data){style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}

::: {.notes}
Two and a half minutes. The second gate, and a different kind of thing.

A data-use agreement governs somebody else's proprietary data. It is
negotiated by lawyers on both sides. At Cornell the Office of Sponsored
Programs is the party that enters into agreements for the use of data, and
its page says so. You are not a party. You cannot accept a firm's terms on
the team's behalf, however reasonable they look.

Is it legally binding? Yes. It binds the university, and you are bound
through the university, so a breach is a matter between the firm and Cornell
first and between Cornell and you second. The firm's remedy is against the
institution, and the institution's remedy is against the person who
breached.

The last bullet is honest. OSP's page speaks of investigators. Whether it
signs for a capstone team with a faculty advisor is a question, and the
team that needs the answer asks it in October.
:::

## What the clauses do

- Publication review is normal and a veto is not, so settle it before anybody signs.
- Destruction at the end, no redistribution, and no attempt to re-identify are standard.
- The agreement names who may touch the file and where it may live.
- Most of what Cornell licenses is for academic non-commercial use, WRDS and Compustat included.
- A project a firm would pay for cannot be built on a licence that forbids commercial use.

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Read the clauses as things that will happen to your project.

Publication review means the firm sees the write-up before it goes out and
can ask for its confidential figures to be removed. A veto means the firm
can stop the write-up. Review is normal. A veto means you may not be able to
show your own result, and it is settled before signing or the project has no
result.

Destruction means the file goes at the end of the project, so the handoff
to next year's cohort is not yours to promise. No redistribution means no
teammate's laptop that is not on the list, and no upload to a tool that is
not on the list either, which is the shared card after the break.

The last two bullets are the graft from meeting 3. Last week some of you
took private value seriously: a question one firm would pay for. This week,
check the licence on the file you would answer it with. WRDS, Compustat and
most of what the library pays for are licensed for academic, non-commercial
use. It is not a reason to drop the question. It is a reason to know which
file the commercial version can use, and to say so on the checklist.
:::

## Terms of service are the same species

- Terms of service are a contract you accepted by clicking.
- Scraping is rarely a crime and frequently a breach.
- A court held that scraping public LinkedIn pages was not a computer crime, and the same scraper was later found to have breached the user agreement.
- Prefer the download, then the API, then nothing.
- The vendor's terms decide what you may publish, so read them before the file is on your laptop.

[hiQ Labs v. LinkedIn, Ninth Circuit (2022)](https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2022/04/18/17-16783.pdf){style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}

::: {.notes}
Two and a half minutes. The terms of service are a data-use agreement you
signed without reading, and the same three things are in them: what you may
take, what you may keep, what you may publish.

The LinkedIn case is the one people cite for "scraping is legal". Read it
carefully and it says less than that. The appeals court held that scraping
public pages was not unauthorised access under the computer crime statute.
The breach of contract claim was a separate matter, and the district court
later found the scraper had breached the user agreement before the parties
settled. So: rarely a crime, frequently a breach. Both halves are true at
once.

The order of preference is the practical rule. A download you can cite. An
API is a documented door with a record of what you asked for. A scrape is
the last resort, and next week I break one in front of you.
:::

## Employer data brings its own clauses

- A teammate's employer may offer data under a non-disclosure agreement.
- An NDA that covers the result blocks the presentation in this room in December.
- Settle who owns the output before the file arrives.
- A sponsor may have the right to review and never the right to veto.
- A conflict of interest is disclosed rather than confessed: it tells the reader how to weight your claim and nothing more.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. Several of you have a former or current employer who would
hand over data. Good. Three clauses to settle before it arrives.

The NDA. If it covers the result, you cannot present in this room in
December, and meeting 14 is the pitch. Ask now whether the result can be
shown, and write the answer on the checklist.

Ownership. Who owns the analysis, the code and the write-up? If the firm
owns all of it, the proposal you hand in is the firm's document.

The conflict. A teammate who works for the firm has a stake in the answer.
That is disclosed on the title page in one sentence. It is not a confession
and it does not disqualify the project. It tells the reader how much weight
to put on the claim, and hiding it is what disqualifies.
:::

# 4. Holding the file

## Removing the names is not de-identification

::: {style="font-size:0.84em"}
- ZIP code, birth date and sex together identify 87 percent of Americans uniquely.
- Latanya Sweeney used them to pull the governor of Massachusetts's records out of a de-identified hospital file.
- Netflix released anonymised movie ratings and two researchers matched them to named IMDb reviewers.
- New York released taxi trips with hashed medallion numbers and the hashes were reversed in hours.
- Direct identifiers are the easy part and quasi-identifiers are the file.
:::

[Sweeney (2000), Simple demographics often identify people uniquely · Narayanan and Shmatikov (2008), IEEE S&P · Pandurangan (2014), Of taxis and rainbows](https://dataprivacylab.org/projects/identifiability/paper1.pdf){style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Three stories, and each one is a file somebody in this room
would happily download.

Sweeney, 1997. Massachusetts released hospital discharge records with names
removed. She bought the Cambridge voter roll for twenty dollars, joined on
ZIP, birth date and sex, and mailed the governor his own records. Her 2000
paper puts the figure at 87 percent of Americans uniquely identified by
those three fields.

Netflix, 2006. Half a million users' ratings, names replaced by numbers,
released for a prize. Two researchers at Texas showed that a handful of
dated ratings matched to public IMDb reviews identified people, including
what else they had watched.

New York, 2014. A year of taxi trips released under a records request, with
medallion numbers hashed. The hash was a standard one over a small set of
possible numbers, so a developer reversed every hash in a few hours.

The lesson in one line: the columns that identify people are not the name
column. A vendor that removed the names did the easy part.
:::

## Does this vendor file trip a gate

- A vendor sells a consumer file as de-identified.
- Each row carries ZIP code, birth year and sex.
- Sixty seconds at your table: is there a gate, and what is the honest version?

::: {.notes}
Two and a half minutes. Sixty seconds of table talk, two answers from the
room, then told.

Yes. The tree asks whether you can link a row to a living person, not what
the vendor calls the file, and the previous slide says that you can. So it
goes to the IRB office, whose likely answer is that it is exempt, or not
human research once the fields are coarsened. The honest version is the
same project on three-digit ZIP and five-year age bands, or on the vendor's
own aggregates, and it is decided before the file is opened, not after
somebody has already joined it to something.

A vendor's word for de-identified is a sales claim. A determination comes
from the office.
:::

## Where the file lives is a rule

::: {style="font-size:0.84em"}
- Cornell classifies data as low, moderate or high risk.
- Student records and anything under FERPA sit at moderate risk, and proprietary and licensed data are covered by the same rule.
- Identifiers paired with a name, health records and financial account data sit at high risk.
- Cornell's rule: do not enter data at moderate risk or above into a publicly available generative AI platform.
- The approved tools are listed at the AI Innovation Hub, and next week's session runs on that list.
:::

[Cornell IT, regulated data · Cornell AI Innovation Hub, tools and resources · Cornell guidelines for artificial intelligence](https://innovationhub.ai.cornell.edu/tools-resources/){style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}

::: {.notes}
Two and a half minutes. Where the file lives is not a preference.

Cornell's three levels. Low risk is what the university has published for
the public. Moderate risk is any information used in the conduct of
university business unless it is classified otherwise, and FERPA records
sit there. High risk is the identifiers: a name with a social security
number, a passport number, a bank account, health records.

The AI rule is quoted from Cornell's own page in those words: do not enter
any data classified as moderate risk or above into a publicly available
generative AI platform. The guidelines add that anything you put into a
public tool is treated as public. Proprietary and licensed data are covered
by the same rule.

The approved list is at the AI Innovation Hub and it changes. Next week you
drive an assistant on a file, and the file is one you are allowed to
upload, or the assistant sees column names and five invented rows and the
code runs on your laptop.
:::

## Collect only what you need

- A column you did not need is a risk you did not need.
- Salary expectations and visa status in a survey of your own classmates are two such columns.
- Cornell has a policy on research with Cornell students, and surveying your classmates trips it.
- Asking a person for less is the cheapest privacy protection there is.

[Cornell IRB Policy 15, research involving Cornell students](https://researchservices.cornell.edu/policies/irb-policy-15-research-involving-cornell-students){style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. The privacy rule that costs nothing.

Every column you collect is a column you have to protect, store on the
right system, and one day destroy. A column the question does not need is
pure liability. Visa status in a survey about salary expectations is the
example, because it is the column that could hurt a respondent and the
column the question can usually do without.

Cornell has a specific policy on research where Cornell students are the
participants, because of the pressure a classmate or an instructor can put
on a student to take part. A survey of your own section is the case it is
written for. Recruit outside your section, make participation invisible to
me, and drop what you do not need.
:::

# 5. Integrity

## Three words cover research misconduct

- Fabrication is making up data or results.
- Falsification is changing or omitting data so the record misrepresents the research.
- Plagiarism is presenting somebody else's words, ideas or results as your own.
- A citation that does not exist is a fabrication, whoever or whatever produced it.

[42 CFR 93.103, the federal definition of research misconduct](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-93){style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}

::: {.notes}
Ninety seconds. The federal definition, one line each. It is short on
purpose. It does not include honest error, and it does not include
differences of opinion.

The fourth bullet is the one that is live in this room, and it comes back
in three slides.
:::

## How misconduct gets caught

::: {style="font-size:0.72em"}
| Case | What was wrong | Who caught it and how | The price |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Stapel, 2011 | Invented the data for dozens of papers | Three junior researchers in his own lab reported him | His chair and 58 papers |
| LaCour, 2015 | A survey that was never run | Two graduate students tried to replicate it and found the survey firm had no record | The paper and a job offer |
| The 2012 honesty-pledge paper, 2021 | Fabricated rows in an insurance field experiment | Three bloggers found two fonts in one column | The paper |
| Gino, 2023 | Altered rows in four papers | The same bloggers read the edit history inside the Excel files | Tenure at Harvard, revoked in 2025 |
:::

[Retraction Watch on Stapel · Broockman, Kalla and Aronow (2015) · Data Colada 98 and 109 · The Harvard Crimson, May 27, 2025](https://datacolada.org/109){style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}

::: {.notes}
Three and a half minutes. Read the third column down, not the rows across.
Nobody in this table was caught by a reviewer or an editor.

Stapel. A social psychologist at Tilburg who invented datasets for years.
Three junior researchers noticed the data were too clean and went to the
department head. Fifty-eight retractions, which is the count Retraction
Watch keeps.

LaCour. A 2014 paper in Science on whether a conversation with a canvasser
changes minds on same-sex marriage. Two graduate students at Berkeley liked
it enough to extend it, could not reproduce its properties, and asked the
survey firm, which had no record of the survey. Science retracted it and a
job offer at Princeton was withdrawn.

The 2012 paper. A field experiment with an insurance company on signing an
honesty pledge at the top of a form. In 2021 the Data Colada bloggers
showed that the insurance data had rows in two different fonts, one of
them the duplicated and altered half. Retracted. Say nothing about who
fabricated it, because that is not established.

Gino. A Harvard Business School professor. In 2023 the same bloggers
published four posts showing altered rows in four papers, reading the
calculation chain that Excel keeps inside the file. Harvard investigated,
found misconduct, and in May 2025 revoked her tenure, the first time in
decades. Her defamation claims against the bloggers and Harvard were
dismissed in 2024. Every cell in this row is a retraction notice, a court
ruling or Harvard's own action.
:::

## The file outlives the paper

- Every case was caught by outsiders or juniors.
- Every case was caught from the data file, not from the prose.
- Every case was caught years after publication.
- The price was the job.
- Next week you keep the raw file, one path from raw to result, and a note saying where the raw came from, and this is why.

::: {.notes}
Ninety seconds. The pattern is the lesson.

Nobody was caught by the review process. They were caught by people with
no stake, who asked for the file, opened it, and looked. The file always
looks different from the paper. Fonts, edit histories, means that cannot
exist for integer data, a survey firm with no record.

So the reproducibility habits of next week are not tidiness. They are what
lets an honest researcher show the file and be believed.
:::

## An unchecked error can move policy

- In 2010 Reinhart and Rogoff reported that growth collapses once public debt passes 90 percent of GDP.
- In 2013 a graduate student asked for the spreadsheet and found five countries left out of an average.
- The paper had already been quoted in austerity debates in several countries.
- It was an error and not misconduct, and it was caught the same way.

[Reinhart and Rogoff (2010), AER 100(2) · Herndon, Ash and Pollin (2014), Cambridge Journal of Economics 38(2)](https://doi.org/10.1093/cje/bet075){style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}

::: {.notes}
Ninety seconds. The contrast case. Nobody invented anything.

A formula in Excel covered fifteen rows where it should have covered
twenty. The average that made the 90 percent threshold look like a cliff
was wrong. A graduate student at Massachusetts Amherst asked for the
spreadsheet for a class replication, got it, and found it.

By then the number had been cited by finance ministers. Not misconduct.
Same lesson: the file is what gets checked, and next week's spreadsheet
story is this one's cousin.
:::

## The AI generated it is not a defence

- In 2023 a New York lawyer filed a brief citing six cases that did not exist.
- An assistant had invented them, with plausible names and citations.
- The court fined the lawyers 5,000 dollars, and the defence was that the AI generated it.
- The syllabus says the same thing: undisclosed AI use and a fabricated citation are both integrity violations.

[Mata v. Avianca, S.D.N.Y., opinion and order on sanctions, June 22, 2023](https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/63107798/mata-v-avianca-inc/){style="font-size:0.55em; color:#6b6b6b"}

::: {.notes}
Ninety seconds. The case that is live in this room.

A personal injury suit against an airline. The lawyer asked a chatbot for
precedents, got six, and filed them. Opposing counsel could not find them.
The judge could not find them. The lawyer asked the chatbot whether the
cases were real, and it said yes. The court sanctioned the lawyers and the
firm, jointly, five thousand dollars, and made them write to the judges
whose names had been attached to the invented opinions.

The syllabus rule: AI use is fine and disclosed. A citation you did not
verify is yours, and if it does not exist it is a fabrication. Next week
you learn how assistants produce these, and why the DOI resolving to
something else is the tell.
:::

## Is this misconduct

- A team runs three specifications and reports the one that worked.
- Sixty seconds at your table: is that on the three-words slide, and what is the honest version?

::: {.notes}
Two and a half minutes. Sixty seconds of table talk, two answers, then told.

It is not fabrication or falsification under the definition. Nothing was
invented and nothing was changed. And it is the practice most of the
retracted social science of the last decade was built on, because
reporting the survivor of many tries presents a fluke as a finding.

The honest versions are two. Report all three and say why they differ. Or
write the specification down before you run it, which is what
pre-registration is, and the December proposal is where you do that.

Say why this one is on a slide. In March every team in this room will have
three specifications and one of them will look better. This is the
temptation you will actually face, and the cases on the table were not.
:::

# 6. The calendar

::: {style="font-size:0.7em"}
| Gate | Cornell's clock | So it starts by |
|:--|:--|:--|
| CITI training | Two to four hours, and nothing is issued until everyone has it | September 30, meeting 6 |
| Terms of service and licences | An afternoon of reading | This week, for every source on your map |
| An IRB exemption or expedited review | Three to six weeks after a complete submission | Draft the instrument and consent in October, submit by early November |
| The full board | Four to eight weeks, first Friday of the month | Submit by late October for a January start |
| A data-use agreement | Months, and it may fail | Ask OSP in October, and carry a plan B on next week's sheet |
| AEM 6992 | Starts in late January | Everything above clears before it |
:::

::: {.notes}
Three and a half minutes, and this slide is never cut. Read the third
column bottom to top.

AEM 6992 is where you execute. It starts in late January. A full-board
protocol takes up to eight weeks, so it is submitted by late October, so the
instrument and the consent language are drafted in October, so the
question is settled by the pitch. A data-use agreement takes months and
may fail, so the conversation with OSP starts in October and next week's
sheet carries the plan B. Terms of service take an afternoon and the
afternoon is this week. CITI is two to four hours and it is due September
30.

A team that finds out in February that it needs any of this has lost the
semester it was going to run the study in. That is the argument for holding
this meeting in September, and it is the whole argument.
:::

## Session A · 2:05 to 3:15

The hour has six blocks, and the last one is the point.

### Why the rules exist

Every rule in research ethics was written after a specific failure. The
Nuremberg Code followed the doctors' trial. The Belmont Report followed
Tuskegee, which ran for forty years and was stopped by a reporter rather than
by a scientist. Its three principles, respect for persons, beneficence and
justice, are still the frame every review board applies.

The modern failures are the ones that concern this room, and none of them
involved a needle. In 2014 Facebook changed the feeds of 689,003 users to test
whether moods spread, and
[published the result](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1320040111), with the
terms of service as the consent form. In 2018 a personality quiz taken by
270,000 people reached
[up to 87 million profiles](https://about.fb.com/news/2018/04/restricting-data-access/)
through their friends. The first question for the room is what made the
Facebook study research, when Facebook runs experiments on its feed every day
and nobody calls those research. The answer is that it was designed to produce
generalisable knowledge and it was published. The definition turns on the
intent to generalise, not on whether anybody was hurt.

### The IRB

Two questions decide whether it applies. Is this research, meaning a
systematic investigation designed to produce generalisable knowledge? Are
there human participants, meaning you interact with people or you hold
identifiable private information about them? Teams miss the second half.
Scraped posts count when individuals are identifiable, and so do purchased
consumer records.

Cornell's IRB office publishes the
[decision tree](https://researchservices.cornell.edu/sites/default/files/2019-05/IRB%20Decision%20Tree.pdf)
its own staff use, and it has a branch for class projects. A project whose
sole intent is to meet a course requirement is not human participant
research. A project whose results leave the course, for a publication, a
presentation or a sponsor's decision, is. A capstone is the second kind. A
study whose outcomes stay specific to one organisation is not research
either, which is last week's private value. Existing data has its own tree,
and the question it asks is whether you can link a row to a living person,
directly or through a code, not what the vendor calls the file.

Then the levels of review, in Cornell's own weeks. An exemption takes
[three to four](https://researchservices.cornell.edu/resources/life-cycle-irb-protocol),
expedited review four to six, the full board four to eight, and the board
meets on the first Friday of the month. You do not decide that you are
exempt. The IRB issues that determination, and it issues nothing until every
person named on the protocol has finished
[CITI human-participants training](https://researchservices.cornell.edu/resources/irb-training),
exempt protocols included. So the training is a requirement of this course.
Everyone completes it and uploads the certificate to Canvas before meeting 6,
Wednesday September 30. A student protocol needs a faculty advisor who
answers for it, and that is me, so your draft goes past me before it goes
to the IRB.

### Contracts

A data-use agreement is a contract, not an ethics review, and the university
signs it rather than you, through the
[Office of Sponsored Programs](https://researchservices.cornell.edu/resources/exchange-commercially-unavailablerestricted-data).
Expect legal review on both sides. Expect months. Expect clauses on
publication review, destruction and redistribution, and settle one before
anybody signs: a sponsor may have the right to review, never the right to
veto. Then the clause that catches teams that took private value seriously
last week. Most of what Cornell licenses, WRDS and Compustat included, is for
academic non-commercial use, so a project a firm would pay for cannot be
built on it.

Terms of service are the same species, a contract you accepted by clicking.
Scraping is rarely a crime and frequently a breach. Prefer the download, then
the API, then nothing. And employer data brings its own clauses: an NDA that
covers the result blocks the presentation in December, ownership of the
output is settled before the file arrives, and a conflict of interest is
disclosed rather than confessed.

### Holding the file

[Latanya Sweeney](https://dataprivacylab.org/projects/identifiability/paper1.pdf)
showed that ZIP code, birth date and sex together identify 87 percent of
Americans uniquely, and used them to pull a governor's records out of a
de-identified hospital file. Netflix's anonymised movie ratings were
[matched to named IMDb reviewers](https://doi.org/10.1109/SP.2008.33). New
York's taxi trips, released with hashed medallion numbers, were
[reversed in hours](https://tech.vijayp.ca/of-taxis-and-rainbows-f6bc289679a1).
So removing the names is not de-identification, and a vendor's word for it is
not a determination.

Where the file lives is a rule rather than a preference. Cornell classifies
data as [low, moderate or high risk](https://it.cornell.edu/regulated-data),
and its rule is that nothing at moderate risk or above goes into a publicly
available AI tool. The approved tools are listed at the
[AI Innovation Hub](https://innovationhub.ai.cornell.edu/tools-resources/),
and next week's session runs on that list. Collect only what you need,
because a column you did not need is a risk you did not need.

### Integrity

Fabrication, falsification and plagiarism, one line each, from the
[federal definition](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-93).
Then the cases, with how each was caught and what it cost. The table is
below. The pattern is the lesson: caught by outsiders and juniors, from the
data file, years later, and the price was the job. Reinhart and Rogoff were
not misconduct, but a spreadsheet error nobody checked moved fiscal policy,
and the same file caught it. And the one that is live in this room: a
fabricated citation is a fabrication. A New York lawyer was sanctioned in
2023 for filing six cases an assistant had invented, and the AI generated it
was his defence. The second question for the room is whether running three
specifications and reporting the one that worked is misconduct.

### The calendar

Run backwards from January. That is the argument for holding this meeting in
September.

| Gate | Cornell's clock | So it starts by |
|:--|:--|:--|
| CITI training | Two to four hours, and nothing is issued until everyone has it | September 30, meeting 6 |
| Terms of service and licences | An afternoon of reading | This week, for every source on your map |
| An IRB exemption or expedited review | Three to six weeks after a complete submission | Draft the instrument and consent in October, submit by early November |
| The full board | Four to eight weeks, first Friday of the month | Submit by late October for a January start |
| A data-use agreement | Months, and it may fail | Ask OSP in October, and carry a plan B on next week's sheet |
| AEM 6992 | Starts in late January | Everything above clears before it |

### The cases in full

| Case | What was wrong | Who caught it and how | The price | Sources |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Stapel, 2011 | Invented the data for dozens of papers | Three junior researchers in his own lab reported him | His chair and 58 papers | [Retraction Watch](https://retractionwatch.com/category/by-author/diederik-stapel/) |
| LaCour, 2015 | A survey that was never run | Two graduate students tried to replicate it and found the survey firm had no record | The paper and a job offer | [Broockman, Kalla and Aronow](https://stanford.edu/~dbroock/broockman_kalla_aronow_lg_irregularities.pdf); [the retraction](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aac6638) |
| The 2012 honesty-pledge paper, 2021 | Fabricated rows in an insurance field experiment | Three bloggers found two fonts in one column | The paper | [Data Colada 98](https://datacolada.org/98); [the retraction](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2115397118) |
| Gino, 2023 | Altered rows in four papers | The same bloggers read the edit history inside the Excel files | Harvard revoked her tenure in 2025, and her defamation claims were dismissed in 2024 | [Data Colada 109](https://datacolada.org/109); [The Harvard Crimson](https://www.thecrimson.com/article/2025/5/27/gino-tenure-revoked/) |
| Reinhart and Rogoff, 2013 | A spreadsheet formula that left five countries out of an average; an error, not misconduct | A graduate student asked for the spreadsheet | A number already quoted in austerity debates | [Reinhart and Rogoff](https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.100.2.573); [Herndon, Ash and Pollin](https://doi.org/10.1093/cje/bet075) |
| Mata v. Avianca, 2023 | Six invented cases in a court filing | Opposing counsel could not find them | A 5,000 dollar sanction | [The docket](https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/63107798/mata-v-avianca-inc/) |

### Cornell's pages in one list

- [Does your project require an application to the Cornell IRB office?](https://researchservices.cornell.edu/sites/default/files/2019-05/IRB%20Decision%20Tree.pdf) The two decision trees.
- [The life cycle of an IRB protocol](https://researchservices.cornell.edu/resources/life-cycle-irb-protocol). The weeks, what a submission contains, and the faculty advisor.
- [IRB FAQs](https://researchservices.cornell.edu/resources/irb-faqs). The board's first Friday, and why exempt is a determination.
- [IRB training](https://researchservices.cornell.edu/resources/irb-training). Which CITI course, and how long it takes.
- [Research involving Cornell students](https://researchservices.cornell.edu/policies/irb-policy-15-research-involving-cornell-students). The policy that a survey of classmates trips.
- [Exchange restricted data](https://researchservices.cornell.edu/resources/exchange-commercially-unavailablerestricted-data). The Office of Sponsored Programs and data-use agreements.
- [Regulated data](https://it.cornell.edu/regulated-data). Cornell's three levels.
- [AI tools and resources](https://innovationhub.ai.cornell.edu/tools-resources/). The approved list and the rule on public tools.

## Session B · 3:30 to 4:30

Ten minutes of team check-in, then one shared card. A team holds a licensed
WRDS extract and is about to upload it to a chatbot for cleaning. Every team
answers three questions on paper. Which gate does this trip: the IRB, a
data-use agreement, terms of service, a conflict of interest, integrity, or
none? What is the earliest date it has to start? And the half that carries
the marks: what is the version of this project that is legal, is honest, and
is still worth doing? Then the answer, told once.

Then your own project. You fill in the ethics-and-access checklist for it,
on the template, signed by every member. Human participants, yes or no, with
the branch of the tree that justifies the answer. Every data source you
named, who holds it, and what its licence or terms permit. Whether any field
is identifiable, what you do about it, and where the file will live. Any
conflict, one sentence each, and whether the result can be shown in this
room in December. Who does what, by name. And the date the slowest gate has
to start.

Then every team goes to the front. Two and a half minutes each with a hard
stop: one member reads the gate lines, the room attacks by naming a gate the
team missed, and I rule. Most teams will find they need none of it, and a
team holding a project that trips nothing has to be willing to say so. The
teams that do need something find out today, which is the whole reason this
meeting is in September.

Six more cards are on the handout for practice, and their answers appear on
this page after the meeting.

## Where to read more

[Adams, Khan, Raeside and White](https://doi.org/10.4135/9788132108498),
chapter 2, on research ethics.

[The Belmont Report](https://www.hhs.gov/ohrp/regulations-and-policy/belmont-report/index.html)
is nine pages and it is the frame every review board applies. Read it once.

[Sweeney (2000)](https://dataprivacylab.org/projects/identifiability/paper1.pdf)
is the paper behind the 87 percent, and
[Narayanan and Shmatikov (2008)](https://doi.org/10.1109/SP.2008.33) is the
Netflix paper. Both are short.

[Data Colada](https://datacolada.org) is where the Gino and honesty-pledge
findings were published, post by post, with the files. It is the best
available course in how a data file gives a paper away.
